subject: Biology

mods.t: The nervous system, brain and behaviour

cards: BIO.MONOMER
What is a monomer?
A smaller unit that can **join** with many others to form a **polymer**
BIO.POLYMER
What is a polymer?
A large molecule made of **many monomers** joined together
BIO.CONDENSATION
What is a condensation reaction?
A reaction that **joins two molecules** with a chemical bond and **releases a molecule of water**
BIO.HYDROLYSIS
What is a hydrolysis reaction?
A reaction that **breaks a chemical bond** between two molecules using a molecule of **water**
BIO.GLYCOSIDIC
Name the bond formed between two monosaccharides.
A **glycosidic bond**, formed by a **condensation** reaction
BIO.DISACCHARIDES
Which monosaccharides make maltose, sucrose and lactose?
Maltose is **glucose + glucose**; sucrose is **glucose + fructose**; lactose is **glucose + galactose**
BIO.ALPHA_BETA
How do alpha and beta glucose differ?
On **carbon 1**, the OH group is **below** the ring in alpha glucose and **above** the ring in beta glucose
BIO.STARCH
How is starch suited to storing energy in plants?
It is a mix of coiled amylose, which is **compact**, and **branched** amylopectin, whose many ends are hydrolysed quickly; it is **insoluble**, so it does not affect **water potential**
BIO.GLYCOGEN
How is glycogen suited to storing energy in animals?
It is **highly branched**, so its many ends are hydrolysed to glucose quickly; it is also **compact** and **insoluble**
BIO.CELLULOSE
How is the structure of cellulose related to its function?
Long, straight chains of **beta glucose** are linked by **hydrogen bonds** into **microfibrils**, which give the cell wall **strength**
BIO.REDUCING_TEST
Describe the test for a reducing sugar.
**Heat** the sample with **Benedict's** reagent; a **brick-red precipitate** shows a reducing sugar
BIO.NONREDUCING_TEST
Describe the test for a non-reducing sugar.

After a negative Benedict's test, boil a fresh sample with **dilute hydrochloric acid**, **neutralise** it with sodium hydrogencarbonate, then heat with Benedict's reagent; a **brick-red precipitate** shows a non-reducing sugar
BIO.STARCH_TEST
Describe the test for starch.
Add **iodine** in potassium iodide solution; it turns from orange-brown to **blue-black** if starch is present
BIO.EMULSION_TEST
Describe the emulsion test for lipids.
Shake the sample with **ethanol**, then add **water**; a **milky white emulsion** shows a lipid
BIO.BIURET_TEST
Describe the biuret test for proteins.
Add **biuret** reagent; the solution turns from blue to **purple** if protein is present
BIO.ESTER_BOND
Which bond forms between glycerol and a fatty acid?
An **ester bond**, formed in a **condensation** reaction
BIO.TRIGLYCERIDE
What is a triglyceride?
One **glycerol** molecule joined to **three fatty acids** by **ester bonds**
BIO.SATURATED
How does a saturated fatty acid differ from an unsaturated one?
A saturated fatty acid has **no carbon-carbon double bonds**; an unsaturated one has **at least one**
BIO.PHOSPHOLIPID
How does a phospholipid differ from a triglyceride?
One fatty acid is replaced by a **phosphate group**, which is **hydrophilic**, while the fatty acid tails are **hydrophobic**
BIO.AMINO_ACID
Describe the general structure of an amino acid.
A central carbon bonded to an **amine group**, a **carboxyl group**, a hydrogen atom and a variable **R group**
BIO.PEPTIDE_BOND
Which bond joins two amino acids?
A **peptide bond**, formed by a **condensation** reaction
BIO.PRIMARY
What is the primary structure of a protein?
The **sequence of amino acids** in the polypeptide chain
BIO.SECONDARY
What is the secondary structure of a protein?
The coiling or folding of the chain into an **alpha helix** or a **beta pleated sheet**, held by **hydrogen bonds**
BIO.TERTIARY
What is the tertiary structure of a protein?
The further folding of the polypeptide into a precise **3D shape**, held by **hydrogen bonds**, **ionic bonds** and **disulfide bridges**
BIO.QUATERNARY
What is the quaternary structure of a protein?
The arrangement of **more than one polypeptide** chain in a single protein
BIO.GLOBULAR_FIBROUS
How do globular and fibrous proteins differ?
Globular proteins are compact, roughly spherical and **soluble**, with metabolic roles; fibrous proteins are long, **insoluble** strands with **structural** roles
BIO.ENZYME
What is an enzyme?
A **biological catalyst**: a protein that speeds up a reaction by **lowering** its **activation energy**, without being used up
BIO.ACTIVATION_ENERGY
What is activation energy?
The **minimum energy** needed for a reaction to happen
BIO.INDUCED_FIT
Describe the induced-fit model of enzyme action.
As the substrate binds, the **active site changes shape** slightly to mould around it, putting **strain** on the substrate's bonds and lowering the **activation energy**
BIO.LOCK_KEY
Describe the lock-and-key model.
The active site has a **fixed shape** that is **complementary** to one substrate, so only that substrate fits
BIO.ES_COMPLEX
What is an enzyme-substrate complex?
The structure formed when a **substrate binds** to the complementary **active site** of an enzyme
BIO.DENATURED
What happens when an enzyme is denatured?
High temperature or extreme pH breaks the **hydrogen and ionic bonds** that hold its **tertiary structure**, so the **active site changes shape** and is **no longer complementary** to the substrate
BIO.TEMPERATURE_RATE
Why does an enzyme reaction speed up as temperature rises towards the optimum?
Molecules have more **kinetic energy**, so there are more successful **collisions** and more **enzyme-substrate complexes** form
BIO.COMPETITIVE
How does a competitive inhibitor work?
It has a **similar shape to the substrate** and binds to the **active site**, so fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form; adding **more substrate** reduces its effect
BIO.NONCOMPETITIVE
How does a non-competitive inhibitor work?
It binds to the enzyme **away from the active site**, **changing the shape** of the active site so the substrate no longer fits; adding **more substrate does not** reduce its effect
BIO.COFACTOR
What is a cofactor?
A **non-protein** substance that an enzyme needs in order to work
BIO.COENZYME
What is a coenzyme?
An **organic cofactor**, often made from a **vitamin**, that carries chemical groups between enzymes
BIO.PROSTHETIC
What is a prosthetic group?
A cofactor that is **permanently bound** to the enzyme
BIO.NUCLEOTIDE
What does a DNA nucleotide consist of?
A **phosphate** group, the pentose sugar **deoxyribose** and a nitrogen-containing organic **base**
BIO.RNA_NUCLEOTIDE
How does an RNA nucleotide differ from a DNA nucleotide?
It has **ribose** instead of deoxyribose, and **uracil** instead of **thymine**
BIO.PHOSPHODIESTER
Which bond links nucleotides in a strand?
A **phosphodiester bond**, formed by a **condensation** reaction
BIO.BASE_PAIRS
State the complementary base pairs in DNA.
**Adenine pairs with thymine** and **guanine pairs with cytosine**, held by **hydrogen bonds**
BIO.SEMI_CONSERVATIVE
What is semi-conservative replication?
Each new DNA molecule contains **one original strand** and **one newly made strand**
BIO.HELICASE
What does DNA helicase do?
It **breaks the hydrogen bonds** between the bases, unwinding and **separating** the two strands
BIO.DNA_POLYMERASE
What does DNA polymerase do?
It **joins adjacent nucleotides** of the new strand in condensation reactions, forming **phosphodiester bonds**
BIO.ATP
What is ATP made of?
The base **adenine**, the sugar **ribose** and **three phosphate groups**
BIO.ATP_HYDROLYSIS
How does ATP release energy?
ATP hydrolase hydrolyses it to **ADP** and **inorganic phosphate**, releasing a small amount of energy
BIO.ATP_SUITED
Why is ATP a good immediate source of energy?
It releases energy in **small**, manageable amounts in a **single** hydrolysis step, and it is **quickly re-made**
BIO.WATER_SOLVENT
Why is water a good solvent?
Water is **polar**, so its slightly charged ends surround **ions** and other polar molecules, which dissolve
BIO.WATER_HEAT
Why does water's high specific heat capacity matter to organisms?
**A lot of energy** is needed to change its temperature, so it **buffers temperature changes** in cells and habitats
BIO.SWEATING
Why does sweating cool the body?
Water has a **high latent heat of vaporisation**, so evaporating it takes a lot of heat energy from the skin
BIO.COHESION
What is cohesion in water, and why does it matter to plants?
Water molecules attract each other by **hydrogen bonding**, so water is pulled up the xylem as a **continuous column**
BIO.IONS
State a role each for iron ions, phosphate ions and hydrogen ions.
Iron ions are part of **haemoglobin**, **ph**osphate ions are part of DNA, RNA and **ATP**, and hydrogen ions set the pH
BIO.NUCLEUS
What is the function of the nucleus?
It holds the cell's **DNA** and **controls** its activities; the **nucleolus** inside it makes ribosomes
BIO.MITOCHONDRION
What is the function of a mitochondrion?
It is the site of **aerobic respiration**, where most **ATP** is made
BIO.RER
What does the rough endoplasmic reticulum do?
The **ribosomes** on its surface make **proteins**, which it folds and transports
BIO.SER
What does the smooth endoplasmic reticulum do?
It makes and processes **lipids**
BIO.GOLGI
What does the Golgi apparatus do?
It **modifies** proteins and lipids and **packages** them into **vesicles**; it also makes lysosomes
BIO.LYSOSOME
What is a lysosome?
A vesicle of **hydrolytic enzymes** that break down pathogens and worn-out organelles
BIO.RIBOSOME
What is a ribosome, and how do ribosomes differ between cells?
The site of **protein synthesis**: **80S** in eukaryotic cytoplasm, and the smaller **70S** in prokaryotes, mitochondria and chloroplasts
BIO.CHLOROPLAST
What does a chloroplast do?
It is the site of **photosynthesis**: its **thylakoids** hold chlorophyll for the light-dependent reaction, and the **stroma** is where the light-independent reaction happens
BIO.CELL_WALL
What is a plant cell wall made of, and what does it do?
It is made of **cellulose** and gives the cell **strength** and support, stopping it bursting when it takes in water
BIO.VACUOLE
What does the permanent vacuole do in a plant cell?
It holds **cell sap** and keeps the cell **turgid**
BIO.PROKARYOTE
How does a prokaryotic cell differ from a eukaryotic cell?
It has **no nucleus** and no **membrane-bound organelles**, smaller **70S ribosomes**, a murein cell wall, and **circular DNA** not associated with histones
BIO.PLASMID
What is a plasmid?
A **small ring of DNA** in a prokaryote, **separate** from the main chromosome, often carrying genes such as antibiotic resistance
BIO.VIRUS
Describe the structure of a virus.
A non-living particle: **genetic material**, DNA or RNA, inside a protein coat called a **capsid**, with **attachment proteins** on its surface
BIO.MAGNIFICATION
How is magnification calculated?
Magnification = **size of image** ÷ **size of real object**
BIO.RESOLUTION
What is resolution in microscopy?
The **minimum distance** between two points at which they can still be seen as **separate**
BIO.TEM_SEM
How does a TEM image differ from an SEM image?
A TEM passes electrons **through a thin specimen**, giving a **2D** image of internal structure at the highest resolution; an SEM **scans** electrons across the surface, giving a **3D** image
BIO.ELECTRON_MICROSCOPE
Why does an electron microscope resolve more detail than a light microscope?
Electrons have a much **shorter wavelength** than light
BIO.FRACTIONATION_PREP
Why is tissue kept cold, isotonic and buffered for cell fractionation?
**Cold** to slow **enzymes** that would digest the organelles, **isotonic** so organelles do not burst or shrink by **osmosis**, and **buffered** so pH changes do not denature proteins
BIO.ULTRACENTRIFUGE
In what order do organelles separate in differential centrifugation?
The densest first as the speed rises: **nuclei**, then chloroplasts, then **mitochondria**, with **ribosomes last**
BIO.STAINING
Why are specimens stained for light microscopy?
To increase **contrast**, so structures that would otherwise be transparent can be seen
BIO.CYTOSKELETON
What does the cytoskeleton do?
Its protein microfilaments and **microtubules** **support** the cell, **move** organelles and vesicles, and move cilia and flagella
BIO.PROTEIN_ROUTE
Describe the route of a protein made for secretion.

It is made on ribosomes on the **rough ER**, carried in a **vesicle** to the **Golgi apparatus** to be modified and packaged, then carried in a vesicle to the cell surface membrane and released by **exocytosis**
BIO.CELL_CYCLE
Name the stages of the cell cycle.
**Interphase**, when the cell grows and its **DNA replicates** (G1, S and G2), then **mitosis**, then **cytokinesis**
BIO.MITOSIS
What is mitosis?
Nuclear division that produces two **genetically identical** nuclei, each with the **same number of chromosomes** as the parent
BIO.PROPHASE
What happens in prophase?
The chromosomes **condense** and become visible, the **nuclear envelope breaks down**, and **spindle** fibres begin to form
BIO.METAPHASE
What happens in metaphase?
The chromosomes **line up** on the **equator** of the cell, attached to spindle fibres by their **centromeres**
BIO.ANAPHASE
What happens in anaphase?
The **centromeres divide** and the spindle fibres shorten, pulling the **sister chromatids** to **opposite poles**
BIO.TELOPHASE
What happens in telophase?
The chromatids reach the **poles** and uncoil, and a **nuclear envelope forms** around each set
BIO.MITOTIC_INDEX
How is the mitotic index calculated?
The **number of cells in mitosis** divided by the **total number of cells** seen
BIO.BINARY_FISSION
Describe binary fission.
The **circular DNA** and any plasmids **replicate**, the cell grows, and the cytoplasm divides into **two daughter cells**, each with a copy of the circular DNA
BIO.VIRAL_REPLICATION
How do viruses replicate?
**Attachment proteins** bind to receptors on a **host cell**, the viral genetic material enters it, and the host cell's machinery makes **new viral particles**
BIO.TUMOUR
What is a tumour, and what causes it?
A mass of cells made by **uncontrolled** mitosis, caused by **mutations** in the genes that regulate **cell division**
BIO.CANCER_DRUGS
How do many cancer drugs work?
They disrupt the **cell cycle**, for example by stopping **DNA replication** or **spindle** formation, so the fast-dividing cancer cells cannot divide
BIO.CHECKPOINTS
What are the checkpoints in the cell cycle?
Points where the cell **checks** that conditions are right, such as the **DNA** being undamaged and fully replicated, before it moves on to the **next phase**
BIO.FLUID_MOSAIC
Why is the membrane model called fluid mosaic?
Fluid because the **phospholipids** and proteins can **move** sideways in the bilayer; mosaic because **proteins are scattered** through it like tiles
BIO.CHOLESTEROL
What does cholesterol do in a membrane?
It binds to the phospholipid tails and **restricts** their movement, making the membrane **less fluid** and more stable
BIO.GLYCOPROTEIN
What do glycoproteins and glycolipids do in the membrane?
They act as **receptors** and antigens, for cell signalling and **cell recognition**
BIO.DIFFUSION
Define diffusion.
The **net movement** of particles from a region of **higher concentration** to a region of **lower concentration**; it is **passive**
BIO.FACILITATED
What is facilitated diffusion?
The **passive** movement of ions or large polar molecules **down a concentration gradient** through **channel or carrier proteins**
BIO.OSMOSIS
Define osmosis.
The net movement of **water** molecules from a region of **higher water potential** to a region of **lower water potential** across a **partially permeable membrane**
BIO.WATER_POTENTIAL
What is water potential?
The tendency of water to move out of a solution, in kPa; **pure water** has the highest value, **0 kPa**, and dissolving solutes makes it **more negative**
BIO.ACTIVE_TRANSPORT
Define active transport.
The movement of molecules or ions **against a concentration gradient**, through **carrier proteins**, using energy from **ATP**
BIO.COTRANSPORT
How is glucose absorbed by co-transport in the ileum?

**Sodium ions** are **actively** transported out of the epithelial cell into the blood, so sodium ions diffuse in from the lumen through a **co-transporter** protein, bringing glucose with them **against its concentration gradient**
BIO.CYTOSIS
What are endocytosis and exocytosis?
Endocytosis takes substances into the cell in **vesicles** formed from the cell surface membrane; exocytosis releases substances when vesicles **fuse** with it; both need **ATP**
BIO.PERMEABILITY
How does a high temperature affect membrane permeability?
Phospholipids gain **kinetic energy** and move more, and membrane proteins **denature**, so the membrane becomes **more permeable**
BIO.PATHOGEN
What is a pathogen?
A microorganism that **causes disease**
BIO.ANTIGEN
What is an antigen?
A molecule, usually a **protein** on a cell's surface, that triggers an **immune response**
BIO.ANTIBODY
What is an antibody?
A protein made by **plasma cells** that binds to one **specific**, **complementary** antigen
BIO.ANTIBODY_STRUCTURE
Describe the structure of an antibody.
**Four polypeptide chains**, two heavy and two light, held by disulfide bridges; the **variable regions** form the **antigen-binding sites**
BIO.AGGLUTINATION
What is agglutination?
Antibodies bind several pathogens together into **clumps**, which **phagocytes** can engulf more easily
BIO.PHAGOCYTOSIS
Describe phagocytosis.
A phagocyte **engulfs** the pathogen into a **phagosome**, and a **lysosome** fuses with it, releasing **lysozymes** that digest the pathogen
BIO.APC
What is an antigen-presenting cell?
A cell that **displays** a pathogen's **antigens** on its own surface membrane, so **T cells** can recognise them
BIO.CELLULAR_RESPONSE
Describe the cellular response.

A **helper T cell** with a **complementary receptor** binds to the presented antigen and divides by mitosis; its clones activate **cytotoxic T cells**, stimulate **B cells** and phagocytes, and form memory cells
BIO.HUMORAL_RESPONSE
Describe the humoral response.
A **B cell** with a complementary antibody binds the antigen, is activated by a **helper T cell**, and divides by mitosis into **plasma cells**, which secrete antibodies, and **memory cells**
BIO.CLONAL_SELECTION
What is clonal selection?
The lymphocyte whose receptor is **complementary** to the antigen is selected and **divides by mitosis** into many identical copies
BIO.SECONDARY_RESPONSE
Why is the secondary immune response faster than the primary?
**Memory cells** remain after the first infection, so they recognise the antigen at once and **divide rapidly** into plasma cells, making **more antibodies** sooner
BIO.ACTIVE_PASSIVE
What is the difference between active and passive immunity?

In active immunity the body **makes its own antibodies** and **memory cells** after meeting an antigen, so it lasts; in passive immunity antibodies are **given from outside**, with no memory cells, so it is **short-lived**
BIO.VACCINE
How does a vaccine give immunity?
It contains **antigens**, often on dead or weakened pathogens, that trigger a **primary response**, so **memory cells** are made without the disease
BIO.HERD_IMMUNITY
What is herd immunity?
When **enough of a population** is vaccinated, the pathogen **cannot spread** easily, so people who are not vaccinated are protected too
BIO.ANTIGENIC_VARIABILITY
Why does antigenic variability make vaccination harder?
The pathogen's **antigens change** shape by **mutation**, so memory cells and antibodies from earlier exposure are **no longer complementary**
BIO.MONOCLONAL
What is a monoclonal antibody?
An antibody made by a **single clone** of plasma cells, so every copy is **identical** and binds to **one specific antigen**
BIO.ELISA
What does an ELISA test detect?
An **antigen or an antibody** in a sample, using an antibody linked to an **enzyme** that causes a **colour change**
BIO.HIV
How does HIV cause AIDS?
HIV infects and destroys **helper T cells**, so the **immune system** cannot respond to other infections
BIO.INFLAMMATION
What is the inflammatory response?
Damaged tissue releases **histamine**, which **dilates** blood vessels and makes capillaries **more permeable**, so more phagocytes and fluid reach the site
BIO.OPSONIN
What is an opsonin?
A molecule that binds to a pathogen and **tags** it, so **phagocytes** recognise and engulf it more easily
BIO.PENICILLIN
How does penicillin kill bacteria?
It stops the bacterium building its **cell wall** properly, so water enters by **osmosis** and the cell **bursts**
BIO.BACTERICIDAL
What is the difference between bactericidal and bacteriostatic antibiotics?
Bactericidal antibiotics **kill bacteria**; bacteriostatic antibiotics **stop them growing** and dividing, so the immune system can clear them
BIO.ANTIBIOTIC_RESISTANCE
How does antibiotic resistance spread through a population of bacteria?
A **random mutation** gives a bacterium resistance; when the antibiotic is used it **survives and reproduces**, passing on the **allele**, so resistant bacteria become more common
BIO.PLANT_DEFENCES
Name two physical defences a plant uses against pathogens.
**Callose** deposited in cell walls and sieve plates, and a **waxy cuticle**
BIO.TRANSMISSION
Give two conditions that increase the spread of communicable disease.
**Overcrowded** living conditions, and **poor hygiene** or sanitation
BIO.NEW_MEDICINES
Why does conserving biodiversity matter for new medicines?
Many medicines come from **wild organisms**, and species **not yet studied** may hold useful compounds
BIO.SA_VOLUME
Why do larger organisms need specialised exchange surfaces?
They have a **smaller surface area to volume ratio** and longer **diffusion distances**, so diffusion across the body surface is too slow
BIO.EXCHANGE_FEATURES
What makes an exchange surface efficient?
A **large surface area**, a **short diffusion distance**, and a **steep concentration gradient** kept up by a good blood supply or ventilation
BIO.ALVEOLI
How are alveoli adapted for gas exchange?

There are millions of them, giving a **large surface area**; their walls are **one cell thick**, giving a short diffusion distance; and a dense **capillary network** keeps a steep concentration gradient
BIO.INSPIRATION
Describe breathing in.

The **external intercostal muscles contract**, lifting the ribs up and out, and the **diaphragm contracts** and flattens, so the **volume** of the thorax rises, its **pressure** falls below atmospheric, and air flows in
BIO.EXPIRATION
Describe breathing out at rest.
The external intercostal muscles and the diaphragm **relax**, so the **volume** of the thorax falls, its **pressure rises** above atmospheric, and air is forced out
BIO.TIDAL_VOLUME
Define tidal volume.
The volume of air breathed in or out in **one normal breath** **at rest**
BIO.VITAL_CAPACITY
Define vital capacity.
The **largest volume** of air that can be breathed out after the **deepest** possible breath in
BIO.PVR
How is pulmonary ventilation rate calculated?
**Tidal volume** × **breathing rate**
BIO.COUNTER_CURRENT
Why is counter-current flow efficient in fish gills?
Blood and water flow in **opposite directions**, so a **concentration gradient** is kept along the **whole length** of the lamellae
BIO.INSECT_GAS
How do gases reach an insect's cells?
Air enters through **spiracles** and moves along **tracheae** and **tracheoles** directly to the respiring tissues
BIO.LEAF_GAS
How is a leaf adapted for gas exchange?
Many **stomata**, **air spaces** in the spongy mesophyll, and thin leaves all give **short diffusion distances** to the cells
BIO.XEROPHYTE
How are xerophytes adapted to reduce water loss?
A **thick waxy cuticle**, **sunken stomata**, **hairs** and **rolled leaves** that trap moist air, and fewer stomata
BIO.HYDROPHYTE
Give two adaptations of a hydrophyte.
Stomata on the **upper surface** of floating leaves, and large **air spaces** that keep the leaves afloat
BIO.STARCH_DIGESTION
Describe the digestion of starch.
**Amylase** from the salivary glands and pancreas hydrolyses starch to **maltose**; **maltase** bound to the ileum's membrane hydrolyses maltose to **glucose**
BIO.PROTEASES
Name the three kinds of protease and what each does.
**Endopeptidases** hydrolyse peptide bonds within a protein, **exopeptidases** remove amino acids from the ends, and membrane-bound **dipeptidases** split dipeptides into amino acids
BIO.LIPID_DIGESTION
How are lipids digested?
**Bile salts** **emulsify** lipids into small droplets, giving a large surface area for **lipase** to hydrolyse them into **monoglycerides and fatty acids**
BIO.MICELLES
What are micelles, and what do they do?
Tiny droplets of **bile salts**, **monoglycerides** and fatty acids that carry these to the epithelial cells of the **ileum** to be absorbed
BIO.HAEMOGLOBIN
Describe haemoglobin.
A protein with quaternary structure: **four polypeptide chains**, each with a **haem group** containing **iron** that binds oxygen
BIO.COOPERATIVE
Why is the oxygen dissociation curve S-shaped?
Once the first oxygen binds, haemoglobin **changes shape**, making it **easier** for the next ones to bind: **cooperative binding**
BIO.BOHR
What is the Bohr effect?
A higher partial pressure of **carbon dioxide** lowers haemoglobin's **affinity** for oxygen, moving the dissociation curve **to the right**, so more oxygen is **unloaded** to respiring tissues
BIO.FETAL_HB
Why does fetal haemoglobin have a higher affinity for oxygen than adult haemoglobin?
So it can **load oxygen** from the mother's blood at the **placenta**, where the partial pressure of oxygen is low
BIO.CO2_TRANSPORT
How is most carbon dioxide carried in the blood?
As **hydrogencarbonate ions**: **carbonic anhydrase** in red blood cells joins carbon dioxide and water into **carbonic acid**, which dissociates into hydrogen ions and hydrogencarbonate ions
BIO.CHLORIDE_SHIFT
What is the chloride shift?
**Hydrogencarbonate ions** diffuse out of the red blood cell into the plasma, and **chloride ions** diffuse in to balance the **charge**
BIO.NEED_TRANSPORT
Why do large multicellular animals need a mass transport system?
Their small **surface area to volume ratio** and long **diffusion** distances mean diffusion alone cannot supply every cell fast enough
BIO.DOUBLE_CIRCULATION
What is a double circulatory system?
The blood passes **through the heart twice** in each complete circuit: once to the lungs and once to the rest of the body
BIO.CLOSED_CIRCULATION
What is a closed circulatory system?
One in which the blood stays **inside vessels** all the way round
BIO.ATRIAL_SYSTOLE
What happens in atrial systole?
The **atria contract** with the **atrioventricular valves** open, pushing the remaining blood into the **ventricles**
BIO.VENTRICULAR_SYSTOLE
What happens in ventricular systole?
The **ventricles contract**; their pressure rises above the atria, closing the **atrioventricular valves**, then above the arteries, opening the **semilunar valves** so blood leaves
BIO.DIASTOLE
What happens in diastole?
The heart muscle **relaxes**, the **semilunar valves close**, and blood from the veins **fills** the atria and ventricles
BIO.VALVES
What makes the heart's valves open and close?
Differences in **pressure**: a valve opens when the pressure behind it is higher and closes when the pressure in front is higher, stopping **backflow**
BIO.CARDIAC_OUTPUT
How is cardiac output calculated?
Cardiac output = **stroke volume** × **heart rate**
BIO.ARTERY
How is an artery adapted to its function?
**Thick** walls of muscle and **elastic tissue** withstand and even out the **high pressure**, around a narrow lumen with a folded endothelium that can stretch
BIO.VEIN
How is a vein adapted to its function?
A **wide lumen**, thin walls with little elastic tissue, and **valves** that stop blood flowing backwards at low pressure
BIO.CAPILLARY
How is a capillary adapted to its function?
Its wall is **one endothelial cell thick**, giving a **short diffusion distance**, and its narrow lumen slows the blood and brings it close to cells
BIO.TISSUE_FLUID
How is tissue fluid formed?
At the **arterial end** of a capillary the **hydrostatic pressure** is high, so fluid is **forced out** into the spaces between cells; large proteins and cells stay in the blood
BIO.TISSUE_FLUID_RETURN
How does tissue fluid return to the blood?
At the **venous end** the hydrostatic pressure has fallen and the blood's water potential is lower, so water moves back in by **osmosis**; excess drains into the **lymph**
BIO.ATHEROMA
How does an atheroma form?
Damage to an artery's **endothelium** triggers an **inflammatory response**; white blood cells and lipids build up under it into a fatty **plaque** that **narrows** the lumen
BIO.CLOTTING
Describe how blood clots.

Damaged tissue and platelets release **thromboplastin**, which catalyses the change of **prothrombin** to **thrombin**; thrombin converts soluble **fibrinogen** to insoluble **fibrin**, which traps blood cells
BIO.MYOCARDIAL_INFARCTION
What causes a myocardial infarction?
A blockage in a **coronary artery**, so part of the heart muscle is starved of **oxygen** and dies
BIO.RISK_FACTOR
What is a risk factor?
Anything that **increases the chance** of developing a disease
BIO.CORRELATION
Does a correlation show that one factor causes another?
No: a correlation shows the two **change together**, but a causal link needs a **mechanism** or a **controlled experiment**
BIO.LDL_HDL
How do LDLs and HDLs differ?
LDLs carry cholesterol **from the liver** to the tissues, and high levels raise the risk of atheroma; HDLs carry cholesterol **back to the liver** and lower the risk
BIO.BLOOD_PRESSURE
What does a blood pressure of 120/80 mmHg mean?
120 mmHg is the **systolic** pressure, when the ventricles contract; 80 mmHg is the **diastolic** pressure, when the heart relaxes
BIO.STATINS
How do statins lower blood cholesterol?
They **inhibit** an **enzyme** the **liver** uses to make cholesterol
BIO.ANTICOAGULANTS
What do anticoagulants do, and what is their main risk?
They **reduce blood clotting**, lowering the risk of thrombosis, but they can cause excessive **bleeding**
BIO.BMI
How is body mass index calculated?
**Body mass** in kg ÷ (**height** in m)²
BIO.MYOGENIC
What does it mean that cardiac muscle is myogenic?
It contracts on its own, **without** needing a **nerve impulse**
BIO.HEARTBEAT
Describe how a heartbeat is coordinated.

The **sinoatrial node** sends a wave of excitation across the atria, which contract; the **atrioventricular node** delays it, then passes it down the **bundle of His** to the **Purkyne fibres**, so the ventricles contract from the **apex** upwards
BIO.AVN_DELAY
Why does the atrioventricular node delay the wave of excitation?
So the **atria** finish contracting and emptying **before the ventricles contract**
BIO.HEART_RATE_UP
How does the brain speed up the heart when blood pressure falls or carbon dioxide rises?
Receptors send impulses to the **medulla**, which sends more impulses along **sympathetic** neurones to the **sinoatrial node**
BIO.ECG
What do the P wave, QRS complex and T wave of an ECG show?
The P wave is the **atria depolarising**, the QRS complex is the **ventricles depolarising**, and the T wave is the ventricles **repolarising**
BIO.XYLEM
How are xylem vessels adapted to carry water?
Long, hollow tubes of dead cells with **no end walls**, walls strengthened with **lignin**, and **pits** that let water move sideways
BIO.COHESION_TENSION
Explain the cohesion-tension theory.
Water **evaporates** from the leaves, creating a **tension** that pulls water up the xylem; **cohesion** by **hydrogen bonds** holds the molecules together as a **continuous column**
BIO.TRANSPIRATION
What is transpiration?
The loss of **water vapour** from a plant's leaves, mostly through the **stomata**
BIO.TRANSPIRATION_FACTORS
Name four factors that increase the rate of transpiration.
Higher **light intensity**, higher **temperature**, lower **humidity** and more **air movement**
BIO.POTOMETER
What does a potometer measure?
The rate of **water uptake** by a shoot, used as an **estimate** of the rate of transpiration
BIO.APOPLAST
What are the apoplast and symplast pathways?
In the apoplast pathway water moves through the **cell walls**; in the symplast pathway it moves through the **cytoplasm**, from cell to cell via **plasmodesmata**
BIO.CASPARIAN
What does the Casparian strip do?
This waxy band in the cell walls of the endodermis **blocks the apoplast pathway**, so water must enter the **symplast**
BIO.TRANSLOCATION
What is translocation?
The movement of assimilates such as **sucrose** from **sources** to **sinks** in the **phloem**
BIO.MASS_FLOW
Explain the mass flow hypothesis.

Sucrose is **actively loaded** into the sieve tubes at the source, lowering the **water potential**, so water enters by **osmosis**; the high **hydrostatic pressure** pushes the sap towards the **sink**, where sucrose is removed
BIO.SIEVE_TUBES
How do companion cells help sieve tube elements?
Sieve tube elements have **sieve plates** and little cytoplasm, so **companion cells**, with many **mitochondria**, make the ATP to load sucrose
BIO.RINGING
What does a ringing experiment show about the phloem?
After a **ring** of bark and phloem is removed, the stem **swells above** the ring, because **sugars** cannot move down past it
BIO.GENE
What is a gene?
A **sequence of DNA bases** on a chromosome that codes for a **polypeptide** or a **functional RNA**
BIO.ALLELE
What is an allele?
A different **version of the same gene**
BIO.LOCUS
What is a locus?
The fixed **position** of a gene on a **chromosome**
BIO.TRIPLET
What is the triplet code?
A sequence of **three bases**, a codon, that codes for **one amino acid**
BIO.DEGENERATE
What does it mean that the genetic code is degenerate?
Most amino acids are coded for by **more than one triplet**
BIO.NON_OVERLAPPING
What does it mean that the genetic code is non-overlapping?
Each base is read as part of **only one triplet**
BIO.UNIVERSAL
What does it mean that the genetic code is universal?
The same triplet codes for the **same amino acid** in **all organisms**
BIO.INTRONS
What are introns and exons?

Introns are non-**coding sequences** within a gene that are removed by **splicing**; exons are the coding sequences that remain
Key words: **non-coding**
BIO.GENOME_PROTEOME
Define genome and proteome.
The genome is the **complete set of genes** in a cell; the proteome is the **full range of proteins** that the cell can make
BIO.DNA_STORAGE
How is DNA stored differently in eukaryotes and prokaryotes?
In eukaryotes it is long, **linear** and wound around **histone** proteins as chromosomes; in prokaryotes it is short, **circular** and not associated with histones
BIO.TRANSCRIPTION
Describe transcription.
**RNA polymerase** joins free RNA nucleotides, complementary to the gene's **template strand**, into a strand of **messenger RNA**
BIO.SPLICING
What is splicing?
The removal of **introns** from **pre-mRNA**, joining the **exons** to make mature mRNA
BIO.TRANSLATION
Describe translation.
Messenger RNA attaches to a **ribosome**; tRNA molecules with complementary **anticodons** bring specific amino acids, which are joined by **peptide bonds**, using ATP
BIO.TRNA
Describe the structure of tRNA.
A single strand folded into a **clover-leaf** shape held by hydrogen bonds, with an **anticodon** at one end and an **amino acid binding site** at the other
BIO.MUTATION
What is a gene mutation?
A change in the **base sequence** of DNA
BIO.SILENT_SUBSTITUTION
Why might a substitution mutation have no effect?
The genetic code is **degenerate**, so the new triplet may still code for the **same amino acid**
BIO.FRAMESHIFT
Why does a deletion usually have a large effect?
It causes a **frame shift**: **every triplet after it** is read differently, changing many amino acids
BIO.MUTAGEN
What is a mutagenic agent?
A factor, such as ionising radiation or certain chemicals, that **increases the rate** of gene **mutation**
BIO.NONDISJUNCTION
What is non-disjunction?
The **failure** of chromosomes or chromatids to **separate** in **meiosis**, so a gamete has one too many or one too few
BIO.MEIOSIS
What is meiosis?
A cell division with **two divisions** that produces **four** **genetically different** **haploid** cells
BIO.CROSSING_OVER
What is crossing over?
In meiosis I, **homologous chromosomes** pair up and **non-sister chromatids** exchange sections of DNA at **chiasmata**, making **new combinations of alleles**
BIO.INDEPENDENT_SEGREGATION
What is independent segregation?
In meiosis I, each pair of **homologous chromosomes** lines up and separates **independently** of the others, so each gamete gets a **random** mix of maternal and paternal chromosomes
BIO.HOMOLOGOUS
What are homologous chromosomes?
A pair of chromosomes, **one from each parent**, with the **same genes** at the **same loci**
BIO.HAPLOID_DIPLOID
Define haploid and diploid.
A haploid cell has **one set** of chromosomes; a diploid cell has **two sets**, one from each parent
BIO.GENETIC_DIVERSITY
What is genetic diversity?
The **number of different alleles** of genes in a population
BIO.NATURAL_SELECTION
Describe natural selection.
A **random mutation** makes a new allele; if it gives an **advantage**, individuals with it **survive and reproduce** more, passing it on, so its **frequency** rises over generations
BIO.DIRECTIONAL
What is directional selection?
Selection that favours individuals at **one extreme** of the range, so the **mean shifts** that way
BIO.STABILISING
What is stabilising selection?
Selection that favours individuals **near the mean**, so the **range narrows**
BIO.ADAPTATION_TYPES
Name the three kinds of adaptation.
**Anatomical** (structure), **physiological** (processes inside the body) and **behavioural** (the way an organism acts)
BIO.SPECIES
Define a species.
A group of similar organisms that can **breed together** to produce **fertile offspring**
BIO.BINOMIAL
What is the binomial naming system?
Each **species** is named by its **genus** and then its species, such as Homo sapiens
BIO.HIERARCHY
List the taxonomic ranks from the largest group to the smallest.
**Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species**
BIO.PHYLOGENETIC
What is phylogenetic classification?
Grouping organisms by their **evolutionary relationships**, from their **common ancestors**
BIO.THREE_DOMAINS
Name the three domains.
**Bacteria**, **Archaea** and **Eukarya**
BIO.FIVE_KINGDOMS
Name the five kingdoms.
**Prokaryotae**, **Protoctista**, **Fungi**, **Plantae** and **Animalia**
BIO.SPECIES_RICHNESS
What is species richness?
The **number of different species** in a community
BIO.SPECIES_EVENNESS
What is species evenness?
How similar the **population sizes** of the different species in a community are
BIO.INDEX_OF_DIVERSITY
Why is an index of diversity more useful than species richness?
It takes account of both the **number of species** and the **number of individuals** of each species
BIO.BIODIVERSITY
What is biodiversity?
The **variety** of living organisms in an area, at the level of **habitats**, **species** and **genes**
BIO.FARMING_BIODIVERSITY
How can farming reduce biodiversity?
Removing **hedgerows**, growing **monocultures** and using **pesticides** and herbicides all reduce the variety of habitats and species
BIO.RANDOM_SAMPLING
Why must sampling be random?
To **avoid bias**, so that the sample **represents** the whole area
BIO.STANDARD_DEVIATION
What does a standard deviation show?
How **spread** out the data are around the **mean**
BIO.MOLECULAR_EVIDENCE
How can DNA or amino acid sequences show how related two species are?
The **more similar** their sequences, the **more closely related** they are, and the more recently they shared a **common ancestor**
BIO.IN_SITU
What is the difference between in situ and ex situ conservation?
In situ conservation protects species in their **natural habitat**; ex situ conservation protects them **outside** it, as in zoos and **seed banks**
BIO.SEED_BANK
How does a seed bank conserve plant species?
Seeds are **dried** and stored **cold** so they stay **viable** for many years, keeping **genetic diversity** for future planting
BIO.NICHE
What is a niche?
The **role** of a species in its **habitat**: everything it needs, and how it interacts with the living and non-living environment
BIO.PEER_REVIEW
How does the scientific community check new evidence?
The work is **peer reviewed** before it is published, then checked by **other scientists** and discussed at **conferences**
BIO.EVOLUTION_EVIDENCE
Give three kinds of evidence for evolution.
**Fossils**, **comparative anatomy** such as homologous structures, and **molecular** evidence from DNA and protein sequences
BIO.REPRODUCTIVE_ISOLATION
What is reproductive isolation?
When two populations can **no longer interbreed** to produce fertile offspring, so their **gene pools** stay separate
BIO.ALLOPATRIC
What is allopatric speciation?
Speciation after populations are separated by a **geographical barrier**
BIO.SYMPATRIC
What is sympatric speciation?
Speciation in the **same area**, when reproductive isolation arises **without a geographical barrier**, for example by a mutation or a change in behaviour
BIO.GENETIC_DRIFT
What is genetic drift?
A change in **allele frequency** **by chance**, which has a bigger effect in **small populations**
BIO.GENE_POOL
What is a gene pool?
**All the alleles** of all the genes in a **population** at one time
BIO.ALLELE_FREQUENCY
What is allele frequency?
**How often** an allele occurs in a population, as a **proportion** of all the alleles of that gene
BIO.HARDY_WEINBERG
What does the Hardy-Weinberg principle predict, and when does it hold?
**Allele frequencies stay constant** from one generation to the next, in a **large population** with **random mating**, **no mutation**, **no migration** and **no selection**
BIO.HW_EQUATIONS
State the Hardy-Weinberg equations.
The two equations **p + q = 1** and p² + **2pq** + q² = 1
BIO.ARTIFICIAL_SELECTION
What is artificial selection?
**Humans choose** individuals with the traits they want and **breed** them, so those alleles become more common over generations
BIO.PHOTOSYNTHESIS_SITES
Where do the two stages of photosynthesis happen?
The light-dependent reaction on the **thylakoid membranes**, and the light-independent reaction in the **stroma**
BIO.PHOTOLYSIS
What is photolysis?
The **splitting of water** by **light** energy into **protons, electrons and oxygen**
BIO.PHOTOIONISATION
What is photoionisation of chlorophyll?
Light energy **excites electrons** in chlorophyll so that they **leave** it, leaving the chlorophyll positively charged
BIO.LDR_PRODUCTS
What does the light-dependent reaction produce?
**ATP** and **reduced NADP**, with **oxygen** as a by-product
BIO.PHOTOPHOSPHORYLATION
How is ATP made in the light-dependent reaction?
Electrons pass along the **electron transfer chain**, releasing energy that pumps **protons** into the thylakoid space; the protons flow back through **ATP synthase**, which makes ATP
BIO.CALVIN_CYCLE
Describe the light-independent reaction.

**Rubisco** fixes carbon dioxide with **ribulose bisphosphate**, making two **glycerate 3-phosphate**; these are reduced to **triose phosphate** using ATP and **reduced NADP**, and most of it regenerates ribulose bisphosphate
BIO.LIMITING_FACTOR
What is a limiting factor?
The factor in **shortest supply**, which **limits the rate** of a process even when others increase
BIO.RF
How is an Rf value calculated?
**Distance moved by the spot** ÷ **distance moved by the solvent** front
BIO.PIGMENTS
Why do chloroplasts contain several pigments?
Each absorbs a **different range of wavelengths**, so **more of the light** energy is captured
BIO.GLYCOLYSIS
Describe glycolysis.
In the **cytoplasm**, glucose is **phosphorylated** using ATP and split into two triose phosphate, which are oxidised to two **pyruvate**, with a **net gain of two ATP** and two **reduced NAD**
BIO.LINK_REACTION
Describe the link reaction.
In the mitochondrial matrix, pyruvate is **decarboxylated** and oxidised to acetate, making **reduced NAD**; the acetate joins coenzyme A to form **acetyl coenzyme A**
BIO.KREBS
What does one turn of the Krebs cycle produce?
Two **carbon dioxide**, **one ATP**, **three reduced NAD** and **one reduced FAD**
BIO.OXIDATIVE_PHOSPHORYLATION
Describe oxidative phosphorylation.

Electrons from reduced NAD and reduced FAD pass along the **electron transfer chain** in the **inner mitochondrial membrane**, releasing energy that pumps protons into the **intermembrane space**; the protons flow back through **ATP synthase**, which makes ATP
BIO.OXYGEN_ROLE
What is the role of oxygen in aerobic respiration?
It is the **final electron acceptor**, combining with electrons and protons to form **water**
BIO.LACTATE_FERMENTATION
What happens in anaerobic respiration in animals?
Pyruvate is reduced to **lactate** by reduced NAD, **regenerating NAD** so that **glycolysis can continue**
BIO.ALCOHOLIC_FERMENTATION
What happens in anaerobic respiration in yeast?
Pyruvate is converted to **ethanol** and **carbon dioxide**, and reduced **NAD** is oxidised back to NAD so that glycolysis can continue
BIO.LACTATE_FATE
What happens to lactate after exercise?
It is carried to the **liver**, oxidised back to **pyruvate**, and mostly converted to **glucose**
BIO.RQ
How is the respiratory quotient calculated?
**Carbon dioxide produced** ÷ **oxygen used**
BIO.RQ_VALUES
What respiratory quotients show carbohydrate and lipid being respired?
About **1.0** for carbohydrate and about **0.7** for lipid
BIO.GPP
What is gross primary production?
The **total chemical energy** in plant biomass made by **photosynthesis**, in a given area and time
BIO.NPP
What is net primary production?
The chemical energy left in plant biomass after **respiratory losses**: **NPP = GPP** − R
BIO.CONSUMER_PRODUCTION
How is the net production of a consumer calculated?
N = I − (F + R): the chemical energy in **ingested** food, minus what is lost in **faeces** and urine and in **respiration**
BIO.TRANSFER_EFFICIENCY
Why is energy transfer between trophic levels inefficient?
Energy is lost as **heat** in **respiration**, and some biomass is **not eaten** or **not digested**
BIO.FARM_ENERGY
How do farmers make energy transfer to livestock more efficient?
By **limiting** the animals' movement and keeping them **warm**, so less energy is used in **respiration** and more goes into biomass
BIO.NITROGEN_FIXATION
What is nitrogen fixation?
The conversion of **nitrogen gas** into **ammonia** or ammonium compounds by bacteria such as Rhizobium
BIO.NITRIFICATION
What is nitrification?
The oxidation of **ammonium** ions to **nitrites** and then to **nitrates** by nitrifying bacteria
BIO.DENITRIFICATION
What is denitrification?
Denitrifying bacteria convert **nitrates** back into **nitrogen gas** in **anaerobic** conditions
BIO.AMMONIFICATION
What is ammonification?
**Saprobionts** decompose the nitrogen compounds in dead organisms and waste, releasing **ammonia**
BIO.MYCORRHIZAE
What are mycorrhizae?
Associations between **fungi** and plant **roots** that increase the **surface area** for taking up water and mineral ions
BIO.PHOSPHORUS_CYCLE
How does phosphorus pass from rock into living things?
**Weathering** releases **phosphate ions** from rock into soil and water, where plants absorb them
BIO.EUTROPHICATION
Describe eutrophication.
Fertiliser **leaches** into water; **algae** grow rapidly and **block the light**, so plants below die; **saprobionts** decomposing them use up the **oxygen** in aerobic respiration, so fish die
BIO.LEACHING
What is leaching?
The washing of **soluble** nutrients such as nitrates **out of the soil** by rain
BIO.CARBON_CYCLE
Which processes move carbon into and out of the atmosphere?
**Photosynthesis** removes carbon dioxide; **respiration**, **decomposition** and **combustion** return it
BIO.GREENHOUSE
How do greenhouse gases warm the Earth?
They **absorb** **infrared** radiation re-emitted from the Earth's surface and re-radiate it, so **less heat escapes** to space
BIO.DENDROCHRONOLOGY
What is dendrochronology?
Reading past climate from **tree rings**, whose **width** shows how good each growing season was
BIO.POLLEN_RECORDS
How do pollen records show past climate?
Pollen is preserved in **layers** of **peat**, and the plants it came from show the **climate** when each layer formed
BIO.ICE_CORES
What do ice cores show about past climate?
**Air bubbles** trapped in the ice layers record past **carbon dioxide** levels, and the ice itself records past **temperatures**
BIO.CLIMATE_MODELS
Why are climate predictions uncertain?
Models **extrapolate** beyond the data and rely on **assumptions** about **future emissions** and feedbacks
BIO.Q10
What is the temperature coefficient, Q10?
The rate at one temperature **divided by** the rate at a temperature **10 °C lower**; about 2 for many enzyme reactions
BIO.DISTRIBUTION_SHIFT
How might climate change alter where a species lives?
As temperatures change, the **range** where conditions suit a species moves, so it may spread towards the **poles** or to higher ground, or die out locally
BIO.SUCCESSION
What is succession?
The change in the communities of an area over time, from **pioneer species** to a **climax community**
BIO.PIONEER
How do pioneer species change their environment?
When they die and decompose they form a thin **soil** and add **nutrients**, making conditions **less hostile** so other species can colonise
BIO.PLAGIOCLIMAX
What is a plagioclimax?
A stable community kept from reaching its climax by **human activity**, such as grazing or mowing
BIO.MARK_RELEASE
How is population size estimated by mark-release-recapture?
Population = number in the **first sample** × number in the **second sample** ÷ number **marked** in the second sample
BIO.MRR_ASSUMPTIONS
What does mark-release-recapture assume?
The marks **do not affect survival** or come off, the marked individuals **mix** back into the population, and there is **no migration**, birth or death between the samples
BIO.BELT_TRANSECT
When would you sample along a belt transect rather than at random?
When studying how a species' **distribution** changes along an environmental **gradient**, such as from a shoreline inland
BIO.BIOTIC_ABIOTIC
Define biotic and abiotic factors.
Biotic factors are the **living** parts of an ecosystem, such as predation and competition; abiotic factors are the **non-living** parts, such as temperature and light
BIO.CARRYING_CAPACITY
What is carrying capacity?
The **largest population** an environment can **support**
BIO.COMPETITION
What is the difference between intraspecific and interspecific competition?
Intraspecific competition is between members of the **same species**; interspecific competition is between **different species**
BIO.PREDATOR_PREY
Why do predator and prey numbers rise and fall in cycles?
More prey lets **more predators** survive and breed, so predators increase and eat more prey; the **prey fall**, then the **predators fall** too
BIO.CONSERVATION_PRESERVATION
What is the difference between conservation and preservation?
Conservation manages an ecosystem so it can be used **sustainably**; preservation protects it from any **human interference**
BIO.SUSTAINABLE
What is sustainable use of a resource?
Using it to meet **present needs** without reducing its availability for **future generations**
BIO.GROWTH_CURVE
Name the phases of a bacterial growth curve.
**Lag**, **log** (exponential), **stationary** and **death** (decline)
BIO.TAXIS_KINESIS
What is the difference between a taxis and a kinesis?
A taxis is a **directional** movement towards or away from a stimulus; a kinesis is a **non-directional** change in speed or rate of turning
BIO.REFLEX
Why is a reflex arc fast?
It involves only **three neurones** and does not need the conscious brain, so the response is **rapid** and automatic
BIO.NEURONE_TYPES
Name the three types of neurone in a reflex arc.
**Sensory**, **relay** and **motor** neurones
BIO.TROPISM
What is a tropism?
A **growth response** of a plant towards or away from a **directional stimulus**
BIO.PHOTOTROPISM
How does IAA make a shoot bend towards light?
IAA moves to the **shaded side**, where it causes **cell elongation**, so the shoot bends **towards the light**
BIO.GRAVITROPISM
How does IAA make a root grow downwards?
IAA collects on the **lower side**, where it **inhibits cell elongation**, so the root bends **downwards**
BIO.PACINIAN
How does a Pacinian corpuscle respond to pressure?
Pressure **deforms** its lamellae and stretches stretch-mediated **sodium ion channels**, which open; sodium ions diffuse in, producing a **generator potential**
BIO.TRANSDUCER
Why are sensory receptors called transducers?
They **convert** the energy of a stimulus into a **nerve impulse**
BIO.RODS
Why do rods work in dim light but give low visual acuity?
**Several rods** connect to **one bipolar neurone**, so their generator potentials add up by **summation** to reach **threshold**, but the brain cannot tell which rod was stimulated
BIO.CONES
Why do cones give high visual acuity?
Each cone connects to **its own bipolar neurone**, so the brain can tell exactly which cone was stimulated
BIO.FOVEA
Why is vision sharpest at the fovea?
It has the highest density of **cones**
BIO.PUPIL_REFLEX
What does the iris do?
It changes the size of the **pupil** by a reflex, controlling how much **light** enters the eye
BIO.RESTING_POTENTIAL
How is the resting potential of a neurone maintained?
Sodium-potassium pumps move **three sodium ions out** for every **two potassium ions in**, and the membrane is **more permeable to potassium**, so the inside is about −**70 mV**
BIO.DEPOLARISATION
What happens during depolarisation?
A stimulus opens **voltage-gated sodium channels**, **sodium ions diffuse in**, and the inside becomes positive, reaching about **+40 mV**
BIO.REPOLARISATION
What happens during repolarisation?
The **sodium channels close** and voltage-gated **potassium channels open**, so **potassium ions diffuse out** and the inside becomes negative again
BIO.HYPERPOLARISATION
What is hyperpolarisation?
The potassium channels are **slow to close**, so too many potassium ions leave and the potential falls **below the resting** value
BIO.REFRACTORY
Why does the refractory period matter?
The sodium channels cannot reopen, so action potentials travel in **one direction** only, are **separate** from each other, and have a **limited frequency**
BIO.ALL_OR_NOTHING
What is the all-or-nothing principle?
Any stimulus above the **threshold** produces an action potential of the **same size**; a stronger stimulus gives **more frequent** action potentials, not bigger ones
BIO.SALTATORY
What is saltatory conduction?
In a **myelinated** axon the action potential jumps from one **node of Ranvier** to the next, so the impulse travels **faster**
BIO.CONDUCTION_SPEED
What affects the speed of conduction along an axon?
**Myelination**, **axon diameter** and **temperature**: a myelinated, wider axon conducts faster, and so does a higher temperature, up to a point
BIO.SYNAPSE
Describe transmission across a cholinergic synapse.

An action potential opens **calcium ion** channels in the presynaptic knob; calcium ions diffuse in, and **vesicles** release **acetylcholine** by **exocytosis**; it diffuses across the cleft and **binds to receptors** on the postsynaptic membrane, opening **sodium ion channels**
BIO.ACETYLCHOLINESTERASE
What does acetylcholinesterase do?
It **hydrolyses acetylcholine** in the synaptic cleft, so the signal stops and the products can be recycled
BIO.SYNAPSE_DIRECTION
Why does a synapse pass signals in one direction only?
The neurotransmitter is released only from the **presynaptic** neurone, and its **receptors** are only on the **postsynaptic** membrane
BIO.SUMMATION
What is the difference between spatial and temporal summation?
In spatial summation **several presynaptic neurones** together release enough neurotransmitter to reach **threshold**; in temporal summation one neurone fires **repeatedly** in quick succession
BIO.INHIBITORY_SYNAPSE
How does an inhibitory synapse work?
Its neurotransmitter opens **chloride ion** channels, so chloride ions diffuse in and potassium ions out, **hyperpolarising** the postsynaptic membrane so an action potential is **less likely**
BIO.NMJ
How does a neuromuscular junction differ from a synapse between two neurones?
It joins a motor neurone to a **muscle**, it is **always excitatory**, and its folded postsynaptic membrane holds more receptors
BIO.SYNAPSE_DRUGS
How can a drug increase transmission at a synapse?
By having a **similar shape** to the neurotransmitter and binding to its **receptors**, or by stopping the **enzyme** that breaks the neurotransmitter down
BIO.SLIDING_FILAMENT
Describe the sliding filament theory.

**Calcium ions** bind to **troponin**, moving **tropomyosin** off the binding sites on **actin**; **myosin heads** bind to form cross-bridges and pull the actin along in a power stroke, then **ATP** lets them detach and re-cock
BIO.SARCOMERE
What happens to the bands of a sarcomere during contraction?
The **I band** and the **H zone** get shorter and the sarcomere shortens, but the **A band stays the same** length
BIO.PHOSPHOCREATINE
What is phosphocreatine for?
It gives its **phosphate** to **ADP** to **regenerate ATP** quickly, for short bursts of contraction
BIO.TWITCH_FIBRES
How do slow-twitch and fast-twitch muscle fibres differ?

Slow-twitch fibres contract slowly for long periods using **aerobic** respiration, with many **mitochondria** and much **myoglobin**; fast-twitch fibres contract quickly and powerfully, tire fast, and rely on **anaerobic** respiration
BIO.MUSCLE_TYPES
Name the three types of muscle.
**Skeletal**, **cardiac** and **smooth** (involuntary)
BIO.ANTAGONISTIC
What are antagonistic muscles?
A pair of muscles that work against each other: as **one contracts**, **the other relaxes**
BIO.HOMEOSTASIS
What is homeostasis?
Keeping the **internal environment** within **set limits**, despite changes outside
BIO.NEGATIVE_FEEDBACK
What is negative feedback?
A change from the **normal** level triggers a response that **reverses** it, bringing the level back towards normal
BIO.POSITIVE_FEEDBACK
What is positive feedback?
A change triggers a response that **increases the change** further
BIO.ECTOTHERM
How do ectotherms and endotherms differ?
Ectotherms rely mainly on their **surroundings** and their **behaviour** to control body temperature; endotherms also make and control heat **internally**
BIO.COLD_RESPONSE
How does the body cut heat loss when it is cold?
**Vasoconstriction** of the arterioles near the skin, **shivering**, raising body hairs to trap air, and less sweating
BIO.THERMOREGULATION_CENTRE
Which part of the brain controls body temperature?
The **hypothalamus**, which detects the temperature of the blood and receives signals from receptors in the skin
BIO.NERVOUS_HORMONAL
Compare nervous and hormonal communication.
Nervous communication is fast, short-lived and targeted, by **electrical impulses**; hormonal communication is **slower**, longer-lasting and widespread, by chemicals carried **in the blood**
BIO.INSULIN
How does insulin lower blood glucose?
It binds to **receptors** on liver and muscle cells, increasing their **uptake of glucose** through more channel proteins and activating enzymes that turn glucose into **glycogen**
BIO.GLYCOGENESIS
Define glycogenesis, glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
Glycogenesis makes **glycogen from glucose**; glycogenolysis breaks **glycogen down into glucose**; gluconeogenesis makes glucose from **non-carbohydrates** such as glycerol and amino acids
BIO.GLUCAGON
How does glucagon raise blood glucose?
It binds to receptors on **liver cells** and activates enzymes for **glycogenolysis** and **gluconeogenesis**
BIO.SECOND_MESSENGER
Describe the second messenger model for adrenaline and glucagon.

The hormone binds to a receptor on the liver cell membrane, activating **adenylate cyclase**, which converts ATP into **cyclic AMP**; cyclic AMP activates **protein kinase** A, which starts glycogenolysis
BIO.INSULIN_RELEASE
How do beta cells release insulin when blood glucose rises?

More glucose enters and is respired, raising **ATP**; ATP-sensitive **potassium channels close**, the cell **depolarises**, **calcium** ion channels open, and calcium ions entering trigger **exocytosis** of insulin
BIO.ISLETS
Which cells of the islets of Langerhans make which hormones?
**Alpha cells make glucagon**, and **beta cells make insulin**
BIO.DIABETES
How do type 1 and type 2 diabetes differ?
In type 1 the **immune system** destroys the beta cells, so **no insulin** is made; in type 2 the cells **stop responding** to insulin, often linked to obesity
BIO.ADRENALINE
What does the adrenal medulla release, and what does it do?
**Adrenaline**, which readies the body for action by raising **heart rate** and **blood glucose**
BIO.ENDOCRINE
What is an endocrine gland?
A gland that secretes **hormones** **directly into the blood**
BIO.ADH
How does ADH control the water potential of the blood?

When the water potential falls, **osmoreceptors** in the **hypothalamus** detect it and the **posterior pituitary** releases ADH, which makes the **collecting duct** **more permeable to water**, so more water is reabsorbed
BIO.AQUAPORINS
How does ADH make the collecting duct more permeable?
It makes vesicles carrying **aquaporins** **fuse** with the cell membrane, adding water channels
BIO.ULTRAFILTRATION
Describe ultrafiltration.

The **afferent arteriole** is wider than the **efferent arteriole**, so the blood in the glomerulus is at **high hydrostatic pressure**; small molecules such as water, glucose and urea are forced into the **Bowman's capsule**, while proteins and cells stay in the blood
BIO.SELECTIVE_REABSORPTION
Describe the selective reabsorption of glucose.
In the **proximal convoluted tubule**, **sodium ions** are actively transported out of the cells into the blood, and glucose is **co-transported** in from the filtrate with sodium ions
BIO.LOOP_OF_HENLE
What does the loop of Henle do?

Sodium and chloride ions are actively transported out of the **ascending limb**, lowering the **water potential of the medulla**, so water leaves the descending limb and collecting duct by **osmosis**
BIO.DEAMINATION
What is deamination?
The removal of the **amine group** from excess amino acids in the liver, forming **ammonia**, which is turned into **urea** in the **ornithine cycle**
BIO.DETOXIFICATION
Name two substances the liver detoxifies, and the enzymes involved.
**Alcohol**, broken down by ethanol dehydrogenase, and **hydrogen peroxide**, broken down by **catalase**
BIO.KIDNEY_FAILURE
Give two treatments for kidney failure.
**Dialysis** and a kidney **transplant**
BIO.PREGNANCY_TEST
How does a pregnancy test detect pregnancy?
**Monoclonal antibodies** bind to the hormone **hCG** in the urine
BIO.GIBBERELLINS
What do gibberellins do?
They cause **stem elongation** and trigger seed **germination**
BIO.ABSCISIC_ACID
What does abscisic acid do in a plant short of water?
It causes the **stomata to close**, reducing water loss
BIO.APICAL_DOMINANCE
What is apical dominance?
**Auxin** from the growing tip of a shoot **inhibits** the growth of **side shoots**
BIO.AUTONOMIC
What is the difference between the somatic and autonomic nervous systems?
The somatic system is under **conscious** control and supplies skeletal muscle; the autonomic system is **involuntary** and controls glands, internal organs and cardiac muscle
BIO.SYMPATHETIC
What do the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems do?
The sympathetic system readies the body for action (**fight or flight**); the parasympathetic system calms it, for **rest** and digestion
BIO.BRAIN_REGIONS
What do the cerebellum and the medulla oblongata control?
The **cerebellum** coordinates movement and **balance**; the **medulla** controls automatic processes such as **breathing** and **heart rate**
BIO.FMRI
What does fMRI show that an ordinary MRI scan does not?
**Brain activity**, by detecting the extra flow of **oxygenated blood** to the regions that are active
BIO.HABITUATION
What is habituation?
A **reduced response** to a stimulus that is **repeated** and **harmless**
BIO.PARKINSONS
What causes the symptoms of Parkinson's disease?
The loss of neurones that make **dopamine**, so less dopamine is released in the brain
BIO.GM_ARGUMENTS
Give one argument for and one against genetically modified crops.
For: **higher yields** or pest resistance can feed more people; against: the new genes could spread to wild plants and reduce **biodiversity**
BIO.STEM_CELL
What is a stem cell?
An **undifferentiated** cell that can divide and **differentiate** into specialised cells
BIO.POTENCY
Define totipotent, pluripotent and multipotent stem cells.
Totipotent cells can become **any cell**, including those of the placenta; pluripotent cells can become **almost any** cell of the body; multipotent cells can become only a **limited range**
BIO.IPS_CELLS
What are induced pluripotent stem cells?
**Adult body cells** made pluripotent again by switching on the genes for particular **transcription factors**
BIO.EMBRYO_ETHICS
Give one argument against using embryonic stem cells.
Obtaining them **destroys an embryo**, which some people believe has a right to life
BIO.DIFFERENTIATION
How does a cell become specialised?
Different **genes** are **switched on or off**, so only some **proteins** are made, and these change the cell's structure and function
BIO.TISSUE
What is a tissue?
A group of **similar cells** working together to carry out a **particular function**
BIO.TRANSCRIPTION_FACTOR
What is a transcription factor?
A protein that **binds** to a specific **DNA** sequence near a gene, switching its **transcription** on or off
BIO.OESTROGEN
How does oestrogen start the transcription of a gene?
It **diffuses** through the cell membrane and binds to a **receptor** on a **transcription factor**, **changing its shape** so it can bind to the DNA and start transcription
BIO.METHYLATION
How does DNA methylation affect a gene?
**Methyl groups** added to the DNA, at cytosine bases, stop **transcription factors** binding, so the gene is **switched off**
BIO.ACETYLATION
How does histone acetylation affect a gene?
Acetyl groups on the histones **loosen** the chromatin, so **transcription factors** can reach the DNA and the gene is **expressed**
BIO.EPIGENETICS
What is epigenetics?
**Heritable** changes in gene function **without any change to the base sequence** of DNA
BIO.RNA_INTERFERENCE
What is RNA interference?
Small RNA molecules bind to **complementary mRNA** and cause it to be broken down or blocked, so it is **not translated**
BIO.ONCOGENE
What is an oncogene?
A mutated **proto-oncogene** that is **permanently switched on**, making cells **divide** uncontrollably
BIO.TUMOUR_SUPPRESSOR
What does a tumour suppressor gene do, and how can it lead to cancer?
It **slows cell division** and triggers cell death; if a mutation or hypermethylation **inactivates** it, cells divide **uncontrollably**
BIO.BENIGN_MALIGNANT
How do benign and malignant tumours differ?
Benign tumours grow slowly, stay in one place and are often enclosed in a **capsule**; malignant tumours grow fast, **invade** nearby tissue and spread by **metastasis**
BIO.HOMEOBOX
What are homeobox genes?
Genes that control the development of the **body plan**, coding for **transcription factors**
BIO.APOPTOSIS
What is apoptosis?
**Programmed cell death**, in which a cell breaks itself down in a controlled way
BIO.LAC_OPERON
How is the lac operon switched on?
Lactose binds to the **repressor** protein, changing its shape so it can no longer bind to the **operator**; **RNA polymerase** can then bind to the **promoter** and transcribe the structural genes
BIO.OPERON
What is an operon?
A group of genes controlled by the **same regulatory** sequence and **transcribed together**
BIO.GENOME_TO_PROTEOME
Why is it hard to work out a complex organism's proteome from its genome?
Much of the genome is **non-coding** or **regulatory** DNA
BIO.BIOINFORMATICS
What is bioinformatics?
Using **computers** to store and analyse biological data such as **DNA sequences**
BIO.PCR
Describe the three steps of a PCR cycle.
Heat to about **95 °C** to separate the strands, cool to about 55 °C so **primers** anneal, then heat to about **72 °C** so **Taq polymerase** extends the new strands
BIO.PRIMER
What is a primer?
A **short** single strand of DNA **complementary** to one end of the target sequence, where DNA polymerase starts
BIO.RESTRICTION_ENZYME
What is a restriction endonuclease?
An enzyme that cuts DNA at a **specific recognition sequence**, often leaving **sticky ends**
BIO.REVERSE_TRANSCRIPTASE
What does reverse transcriptase do?
It makes complementary DNA, **cDNA**, from an **mRNA** template
BIO.LIGASE
What does DNA ligase do?
It **joins** the **sugar-phosphate backbones** of two pieces of DNA, for example sealing a gene into a vector
BIO.VECTOR
What is a vector in genetic engineering?
Something that **carries** the gene into the **host cell**, such as a **plasmid** or a virus
BIO.MARKER_GENE
What is a marker gene for?
It **identifies** the cells that have **taken up** the recombinant vector, for example by antibiotic resistance or fluorescence
BIO.GENE_THERAPY
How do somatic and germ line gene therapy differ?
Somatic therapy changes **body cells**, so it is **not inherited** and may need repeating; germ line therapy changes gametes or embryos, so **offspring inherit** the change
BIO.DNA_PROBE
What is a DNA probe?
A short, **labelled** single strand of DNA **complementary** to a target sequence, used to find it by **hybridisation**
BIO.GENETIC_COUNSELLING
What is genetic counselling?
Advice to people about the **risk** of inheriting or passing on a **genetic condition**, and about their options
BIO.PRENATAL_TESTS
Name two methods of prenatal testing, and their main risk.
**Amniocentesis** and **chorionic villus sampling**; both carry a small risk of **miscarriage**
BIO.ELECTROPHORESIS
How does gel electrophoresis separate DNA fragments?
DNA is **negatively charged**, so the fragments move through the gel towards the **positive electrode**, and **smaller fragments move further**
BIO.FINGERPRINTING
What is genetic fingerprinting based on?
**Variable number tandem repeats**: **non-coding** sequences whose number of repeats differs from person to person
BIO.DOMINANT_RECESSIVE
Define dominant and recessive alleles.
A dominant allele is **always expressed** in the phenotype; a recessive allele is expressed only when **two copies** are present
BIO.GENOTYPE_PHENOTYPE
Define genotype and phenotype.
The genotype is the **alleles** an organism has; the phenotype is its **observable characteristics**, shaped by the genotype and the **environment**
BIO.HOMOZYGOUS
Define homozygous and heterozygous.
Homozygous means having **two identical alleles** of a gene; heterozygous means having **two different alleles**
BIO.CODOMINANCE
What is codominance?
**Both alleles** are expressed in the phenotype of a **heterozygote**
BIO.MULTIPLE_ALLELES
What are multiple alleles?
**More than two alleles** of one gene, as in the ABO blood groups
BIO.SEX_LINKAGE
Why are sex-linked conditions more common in males?
The allele is on the **X chromosome**, and males have **only one X**, so a single recessive allele is expressed
BIO.AUTOSOMAL_LINKAGE
What is autosomal linkage?
Two genes on the **same autosome** tend to be **inherited together**, unless **crossing over** separates them
BIO.EPISTASIS
What is epistasis?
When **one gene** affects the expression of **another gene** at a **different locus**
BIO.DIHYBRID_RATIO
What ratio does a cross between two double heterozygotes give, for unlinked genes?
BIO.MONOHYBRID_RATIO
What ratio does a cross between two heterozygotes give for one gene with complete dominance?
**3 : 1**, dominant phenotype to recessive phenotype
BIO.CHI_SQUARED
When do you reject the null hypothesis in a chi-squared test?
When the calculated value is **greater than the critical value** at p = **0.05**, so the difference is significant and **not due to chance**
BIO.CONTINUOUS_VARIATION
What is continuous variation, and what causes it?
Variation with a range of values and **no distinct categories**, caused by **many genes** and the **environment**
BIO.DISCONTINUOUS_VARIATION
What is discontinuous variation?
Variation that falls into **distinct categories**, usually controlled by **one or a few genes**
BIO.T_TEST
What does a t-test compare?
The **means** of two sets of data, to see whether they differ **significantly**
BIO.POLYMORPHIC
What is a polymorphic gene locus?
A locus that has **two or more alleles**
BIO.VEGETATIVE
Give an example of natural cloning in plants.
**Vegetative propagation**, such as runners, bulbs or suckers
BIO.MICROPROPAGATION
What is micropropagation?
Growing many clones from **small pieces** of plant tissue on a **sterile** **nutrient medium**
BIO.SCNT
How is an animal cloned by somatic cell nuclear transfer?
The nucleus of a body cell is put into an **enucleated** **egg** cell, which is stimulated to divide and then implanted in a **surrogate** mother
BIO.ASEPTIC
Why is aseptic technique used when culturing microorganisms?
To stop **contamination** of the culture by other microorganisms, and of people by the culture
BIO.IMMOBILISED_ENZYMES
Why are immobilised enzymes used?
The enzyme does not **contaminate** the product, it can be **reused**, and it is often more **stable**
BIO.MICROBES_BIOTECH
Why are microorganisms useful in biotechnology?
They **reproduce quickly**, grow on **cheap nutrients**, work at fairly low temperatures, and make products that are easy to separate
BIO.ACROSOME
What is the acrosome reaction?
When the sperm meets the egg, its **acrosome** releases **digestive enzymes** that break down the **zona pellucida**
BIO.CORTICAL
What is the cortical reaction?
After one sperm fuses with the egg, **cortical granules** release enzymes that harden the **zona pellucida**, stopping **other sperm** entering
BIO.FERTILISATION
What is fertilisation?
The **fusion** of the nuclei of a male and a female **haploid** gamete to form a **diploid zygote**
BIO.PLANT_FIBRES
Why are plant fibres strong?
They are made of **cellulose microfibrils** in a net-like arrangement, with secondary thickening of **lignin**
BIO.MINERALS
Why do plants need nitrate, calcium and magnesium ions?
Nitrate to make **amino acids** and DNA, calcium to make **calcium pectate** in the middle lamella, and magnesium to make **chlorophyll**
BIO.DOUBLE_BLIND
Why are drug trials double-blind?
**Neither the patients nor the doctors** know who has the drug and who has the **placebo**, so expectations cannot **bias** the results
BIO.PLACEBO
What is a placebo?
A dummy treatment with **no active drug**, given to a **control group**
BIO.DRUG_TRIAL_PHASES
What is tested in each phase of a clinical drug trial?

Phase 1 tests safety in a small group of **healthy volunteers**; phase 2 tests whether it works in a **small group of patients**; phase 3 compares it with existing treatment or a placebo in **many patients**
BIO.TIME_OF_DEATH
Name three ways of estimating time of death.
**Body temperature**, the degree of **rigor mortis**, and the stage of **decomposition** or the insects present
BIO.RIGOR_MORTIS
What causes rigor mortis?
After death respiration stops, so **no ATP** is made; **myosin** stays bound to **actin** and the muscles stiffen
BIO.ENTOMOLOGY
How can insects on a body show the time of death?
Insect species arrive in a **known order**, and the stage of their **life cycles** shows how long they have been there
BIO.DECOMPOSITION
What affects the rate at which a body decomposes?
**Temperature**, **oxygen** and **moisture**, which change how fast microorganisms respire
BIO.TB_EVASION
How does the bacterium that causes tuberculosis evade the immune system?
It survives **inside macrophages** after being engulfed
BIO.EMERGING_DISEASE
Why do new diseases keep emerging?
Pathogens **mutate**, and more **travel** and contact with animals spread new strains, so existing immunity and medicines may not work
BIO.HOSPITAL_INFECTIONS
How do hospitals limit the spread of antibiotic-resistant infections?
**Hand washing**, **isolating** infected patients, and prescribing **fewer antibiotics**
BIO.KEYHOLE_SURGERY
Why is keyhole surgery used on injured joints?
The **small incisions** cause less damage, so there is less pain and a **faster recovery**
BIO.PED_ARGUMENTS
Give one argument against the use of performance-enhancing drugs.
They give an **unfair advantage** and can damage the athlete's **health**
BIO.VO2_MAX
What is VO2 max?
The **highest rate** at which the body can take in and use **oxygen** during exercise
BIO.SPIROMETER
What can a spirometer measure?
Lung volumes such as **tidal volume** and **vital capacity**, the breathing rate, and **oxygen consumption**
BIO.CONTROL_EXPERIMENT
What is a control experiment for?
To show that **only the independent variable** causes the change, by leaving it out or keeping it constant
BIO.REPEATABLE_REPRODUCIBLE
What is the difference between repeatable and reproducible results?
Repeatable results are similar when the **same person** repeats the method; reproducible results are similar when **someone else**, or a different method, is used
BIO.SERIAL_DILUTION
What is a serial dilution?
A series of dilutions, each by the **same factor**, each made from **the one before**
BIO.ANOMALY
What is an anomalous result?
A result that **does not fit the pattern** of the others
BIO.VALID_CONCLUSION
When is a conclusion valid?
When the method **measures what it claims** to, with other variables **controlled**
BIO.RISK_ASSESSMENT
What goes into a risk assessment?
The **hazards** in a method, how likely harm is, and the steps taken to **reduce the risk**
BIO.COLORIMETER
How is a colorimeter used to find a concentration?
Measure the absorbance of **standard solutions** of known concentration, draw a **calibration curve**, and read the unknown concentration from it
BIO.BIOSENSOR
What does a biosensor do?
It uses a biological molecule, such as an **enzyme**, to detect a substance and give a **signal** in proportion to its concentration
BIO.DISRUPTIVE
What is disruptive selection?
Selection that favours individuals at **both extremes** of the range over those near the **mean**, which can split a population in two
BIO.FINGERPRINT_USES
Give three uses of genetic fingerprinting.
**Forensic** science, testing who is related to whom such as **paternity**, and **medical** diagnosis, as well as plant and animal breeding
BIO.AUTOIMMUNE
What is an autoimmune disease?
A disease in which the **immune system** stops recognising **self** antigens and attacks the body's **own tissues**
BIO.PHOTO_RESP_LINK
How are photosynthesis and respiration linked?
The **glucose** and **oxygen** that photosynthesis makes are what respiration uses, and the **carbon dioxide** and **water** that respiration releases are what photosynthesis uses
BIO.FOUNDER_EFFECT
What is the founder effect?
A few individuals start a **new population**, so its **allele frequencies** differ from the original population's **by chance**
BIO.BOTTLENECK
What is a genetic bottleneck?
An event that sharply cuts the **size of a population**, so the survivors carry only part of the original **gene pool** and **genetic diversity** falls
BIO.ENERGY_BUDGET
What happens when energy intake is greater than energy output?
The extra energy is **stored** as **fat**, so body mass goes up; over time this can lead to **obesity**
BIO.FICKS_LAW
What does Fick's law say about the rate of diffusion?
The rate is proportional to the **surface area** times the **concentration difference**, divided by the **thickness** of the exchange surface
BIO.SCLERENCHYMA
What does sclerenchyma do in a stem?
Its dead cells, with walls thickened by **lignin**, give the stem mechanical **support**
BIO.REFORESTATION
How can reforestation and biofuels lower atmospheric carbon dioxide?
Growing trees take in carbon dioxide for **photosynthesis** and store the carbon; a biofuel releases only the carbon its crop recently took in, so it is close to **carbon neutral**
BIO.ECOSYSTEM
What is an ecosystem?
A **community** of organisms together with the **abiotic** factors of the area where they live, all interacting
BIO.ALTERNATIVE_SPLICING
How can one gene code for more than one protein?
Its pre-mRNA can be **spliced** in different ways, keeping different **exons**, so different mRNA molecules and different proteins are made
BIO.VENTILATION_CENTRE
How does the ventilation centre speed up breathing during exercise?
**Chemoreceptors** detect a rise in carbon dioxide and a fall in blood pH, and the ventilation centre in the **medulla** sends more impulses to the **diaphragm** and intercostal muscles
BIO.PUPIL_BRIGHT
What happens to the pupil in bright light?
The **circular muscles** of the iris contract and the **radial muscles** relax, so the pupil gets **smaller** and less light enters the eye
BIO.NATURE_NURTURE
Why is it hard to tell nature from nurture in brain development?
**Genes** and the **environment** act together, so the evidence comes from **twin** studies, studies of newborns and animal experiments, each with its own limits
